title: Depression, Low Mood & Motivation
description: Explore sadness after disappointment through dialogue, evidence and psychological reasoning.

modules.title: Sadness after disappointment
modules.bookTitle: What low mood is and isn't

lessons.title: When sadness follows a loss
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of sadness after disappointment.

nodes.title: What might be happening?
nodes.body:
Sadness after disappointment is understandable, and time course matters when considering clinical depression. Withdrawal may offer shelter from reminders but also reduce opportunities for comfort and reward. The task is to notice what happens next without rushing from a two-day experience to a diagnosis.

A depressive episode can follow a clear trigger. Duration, severity, other symptoms and functional consequences all require consideration.
nodes.sources: NICE NG222, depression in adults; behavioural activation models.

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: Mara may prefer temporary solitude after disappointment without any unhelpful process.
Mara may be interpreting one painful rejection as evidence of a permanently unsuccessful future.
Mara may be entering a depressive episode that needs further assessment.

checks.explanation: The strongest clues are the character's own words. Mara may be interpreting one painful rejection as evidence of a permanently unsuccessful future. nodes.title: Try a different response
nodes.prompt: The goal is to improve the situation without pretending that you can read the person's mind.
nodes.explanation: A proportionate response deals with the actual situation: Allow space for the loss while making one manageable plan that keeps connection and routine available. Its value does not depend on the other person accepting an interpretation of their motives.
nodes.counterexample: Some situations require independent support or safer channels rather than another direct conversation. A depressive episode can follow a clear trigger. Duration, severity, other symptoms and functional consequences all require consideration.

lessons.title: What would change your mind?
lessons.teach: An initial explanation is useful only if it can be challenged. Revisit the characters, test a rival account and apply the idea in another setting. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Test an account of sadness after disappointment with new evidence and transfer it to a new case.

nodes.title: Two people, different meanings
nodes.prompt: Which conclusion accounts for both perspectives without confusing an interpretation with a fact?
nodes.explanation: Each character can be responding to a different meaning of the same event. The immediate issue is still observable. Understanding both viewpoints helps explain the conflict without requiring both interpretations to be equally accurate.
nodes.counterexample: A depressive episode can follow a clear trigger. Duration, severity, other symptoms and functional consequences all require consideration.

nodes.title: New evidence, new judgement
nodes.prompt: What should happen to your working explanation now?
nodes.explanation: Changing a belief requires comparing the new material with what was already known. The short-term relief followed by isolation suggests withdrawal may be maintaining some of the distress. The new information strengthens some accounts and weakens others; it need not tell us everything.
nodes.counterexample: A depressive episode can follow a clear trigger. Duration, severity, other symptoms and functional consequences all require consideration.
